michigan.headline: 1 Fact, 1 Fiction: Michigan Football vs Ohio State
michigan.body:
ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 24: Head Coach Kyle Whittingham of the Michigan Wolverines speaks to media during the post game press conference after a college football game against the Indiana Hoosiers at Michigan Stadium on October 24, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The Indiana Hoosiers won the game in overtime 13-6. (Photo by Aaron J. Thornton/Getty Images) | Getty Images

One week after upsetting the No. 4 team in the country at The Big House on Senior Day, the Michigan Wolverines now face their final road trip of the season and will take on Ohio State this weekend (Noon on FOX).

Here is this week’s 1 Fact, 1 Fiction.

Fact: The Game is still the biggest game of the year

Just because both teams aren’t where they wanted to be heading into rivalry week, that doesn’t mean this year’s rendition of The Game doesn’t mean anything. Both head coaches are arguably still fighting for their jobs, depending on the outcome, and fans across the country are one loss away from calling their respective season a complete failure.

If Ohio State head coach Ryan Day loses at home to Michigan, it would bring his record against the Wolverines to 2-5, and would mean he lost four of the last five games of the season. The Buckeyes would have their worst season since 2011, a year Michigan beat Ohio State.

If Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham loses to Ohio State, it would prove what Michigan fans have said all year long — he truly hasn’t embraced the tradition and history of the program. The comment Whittingham made about no longer having the “Beat Ohio” drill is definitely disappointing, but it will likely be forgotten if he walks into Columbus and handles business. He will walk into Ohio Stadium with a 6-5 record, the same record as the 2024 squad — and everyone in the college football world remembers how that game went.

Point being, both teams have plenty to fight for. And even if they don’t recognize it, there’s 121 games of history behind The Game that make every year important.

Fiction: Michigan’s offense won’t be enough

Last weekend’s upset win over then-undefeated and No. 4 UCLA proved Michigan’s defense is still one of the best in the country — and surprisingly, that the Wolverines’ offense can be enough to win big games.

Freshman running back Savion Hiter was undoubtedly the MVP on offense in that game with 26 carries for 104 yards. Although he had some negative plays, largely due to poor blocking, he also had some where he stuck his foot in the ground as the Wolverines pounded the rock.

Quarterback Bryce Underwood also had a decent game with 127 passing yards and a touchdown, not including the converted two-point attempt in 3OT. Aside from one fumble by Underwood, it was a relatively clean operation from the offense, and that’s exactly what they’re going to need to replicate in Columbus.

One of the main reasons Michigan’s offense will be enough against Ohio State is because of how dominant the Wolverines’ defense is and the caliber of the Buckeyes’ offense they’re going to face. After quarterback Julian Sayin went down with a season-ending injury, the offense hasn’t been the same for the Buckeyes. Although Michigan’s defense got exposed for some explosive plays against Oregon, aside from that game, the defense has been sound.

In combination with the offense finding a little bit of its footing behind a decent performance from Underwood and strong performance from Hiter and the tight end room, and the defense playing sound football all year long, all the offense needs to do to be enough is what it did against the Bruins — take advantage of good field position and run the ball efficiently.

michigan.headline: Recruiting Roundup: 2 newest commits explains why they chose Michigan Football
michigan.body:
Welcome to the Recruiting Roundup, our twice-per-week series breaking down the latest developments on the recruiting trail for the Michigan Wolverines. We’ll keep you up to date on the top targets, the visits they take, the predictions that analysts make, and everything in between. Here’s what you need to know today…

Michigan’s two-way plans sold Jerrimiah Cross

2028 three-star athlete Jerrimiah Cross grew up rooting for Michigan. When it came time to pick a school, the Wolverines gave the River Rouge junior another reason to stay home. They were one of the few programs willing to give him a shot at both wide receiver and cornerback.

Cross chose Michigan over Michigan State, Arizona State and Virginia Tech on Tuesday, becoming the Wolverines’ first commitment in the 2028 class. The Rivals Industry Rankings list him as the No. 119 receiver nationally and the No. 23 prospect in Michigan.

“I’m comfortable playing wherever the team needs me, but I know they like me at both receiver and corner,” Cross told The Michigan Insider’s Brice Marich.

Cross gave Michigan plenty of film to work with at both spots this fall. He caught 51 passes for 910 yards and 12 touchdowns. At corner, he made 32 tackles, broke up seven passes, forced two fumbles and picked off two passes.

Landon Hall goes from a playoff comeback to a Michigan commitment

Last Friday, Landon Hall had two minutes to erase an 11-point deficit and keep Mishawaka (Ind.) Penn’s undefeated season alive. He pulled it off, leading Penn to a 49-45 win and a spot in the state title game.

The next day, his brothers watched as Kyle Whittingham offered him a scholarship on his first visit to Michigan.

“Their main reason was that I was a winner,” Hall told The Wolverine’s Ethan McDowell.

Hall initially planned to get through Friday’s state championship game before turning his attention back to recruiting. By Wednesday, he’d made up his mind. The three-star quarterback committed to Michigan, joining Kamden Lopati as the second passer in the Wolverines’ 2027 class.

“Getting to experience The Big House and the fans there, it was a pretty crazy environment to be in,” Hall said. “It was definitely the craziest atmosphere I’ve ever been in.”

Through 13 games, Hall has completed 77.6 percent of his passes for 3,253 yards. He threw 51 touchdown passes against just three interceptions and ran for four more scores. Now he gets to play for a state title with his college decision already made.

Cass Tech’s Mylan Griggs explains why Michigan is still in the mix

Detroit Cass Tech’s Mylan Griggs used the fall to see schools farther from home, including UCLA and Washington. The 2028 four-star wide receiver already knew Ann Arbor well after several visits over the past two years, and he still made it back for the UTEP game. Asked what keeps him interested in Michigan, Griggs brought it back to Detroit.

“I’m a city kid, man,” Griggs told The Wolverine’s McDowell. “I love home. I just love home. I believe in them. I think they can change it around.”

Griggs topped 1,000 all-purpose yards, scored nine touchdowns and intercepted four passes as Cass Tech reached the state semifinals. Michigan is recruiting him at receiver, where the Rivals Industry Rankings have him No. 39 nationally at that position. He’s the No. 6 prospect in the state.

He plans to narrow his list now that his junior season is over. Michigan and Michigan State are both in the mix alongside Nebraska, UCLA, Washington and Missouri. Position coach Micah Simon has spent the past year getting to know Griggs, who also stays in regular contact with assistant director of player personnel Richard Perry.

Fee Fi Foe Film: Ohio State Offense 2026

Alex.Drain
November 26th, 2026 at 9:00 AM

Well, it's that time again. The game that everyone spends all year thinking about no one is excited for. Michigan vs. Ohio State. Today we will look at the Ohio State offense, which still features the biggest star in all of college football, but the guy throwing him the ball is different and that matters a lot:

The Film: We have to go with tape from a game after Julian Sayin's injury, which constrains us to the back-half of the season. That's fine, because there are still some solid options to choose from. Oregon is the best (and most comparable by quality) defense that OSU has faced with Luke Fahey at QB, but I already watched that game when I was doing the Oregon defense. So, I wanted to chart something different and have those clips in the back-pocket, which led me to last week's game against Nebraska. The Huskers' defense isn't as strong as Michigan, but it's a decent unit and it's the most recent game, so that's the one I charted.
Personnel: Click for big or HERE for PDF.

Ohio State has a new offensive coordinator. Chip Kelly departed after the 2024 season, leading to a gap year where it was back to Brian Hartline and other in-house options. Then Hartline bailed to be the head coach at USF, so Ryan Day brought in the embattled former Steelers OC Arthur Smith, meaning that both coordinators on this team are guys who most recently worked in the NFL and also the fanbases of the teams they last worked with hate them. Just something to note off the top.
The biggest story for Ohio State's offense in 2026 has been the quarterbacking situation. Julian Sayin was the incumbent starter and and was doing well up until his season-ending injury against Indiana, with 19 TD and 4 INT + 2007 yards and 68.2% completion. Sayin's exit changed the paradigm of the offense by thrusting freshman Luke Fahey into the starter's chair. Fahey was the #586 player in the 247 composite a year ago and has performed admirably considering the circumstances. Limitations, however, remain.
OSU came into the year feeling very good about their RB situation after last season's breakout of Bo Jackson and that good feeling remains. Though the Buckeyes' run game has been spotty against the best opponents, it's not due to Jackson. His speed makes him a major weapon when he gets to the edge and is effective in the pass game as a receiving target too. Isaiah West is the backup, a solid bruiser but not as electric as Jackson. He's also fumbled twice in the last two games. With Ja'Kobi Jackson still injured (hasn't played since mid-October), I wouldn't expect to see much from any other RBs, though freshman Legend Bey makes the occasional appearance.
Ohio State's offenses under Ryan Day have hung their hat on having a series of seemingly unstoppable receivers, and their best outfits had multiple of those on the same team. 2021 famously had three, all of whom have become good NFLers (one of whom is probably the best pro receiver right now). The receiver well is not as plentiful as it once was, such that there is only one of those on this team, but it's the guy who may well give Jaxon Smith-Njigba a run for his money as the best Ohio State receiver in the NFL one day, Jeremiah Smith. His singular brilliance is almost single-handedly keeping the roof up on Ohio State's offense and as of right now, Smith is the betting favorite for the Heisman Trophy.
The situation beyond Smith is rather sketchy. Devin McCuin is the one name who has stepped up, a senior transfer from UTSA who was Third Team All-AAC last season and has had a solid season. But he's not currently looking like a premium NFL draft pick in the mold of Carnell Tate. 6'5 Chris Henry Jr. is the hope to be The Next One in the Ohio State receiver room as a 5* freshman but despite a pair of huge catches in the Indiana game, he hasn't been able to make a consistent, game-changing impact this season. Brandon Inniss was supposed to be a key safety valve on this offense but the trusty veteran hasn't played since Indiana. He's off the injury report now but I'm not sure when he'll get back into a game.
As a result, OSU has been searching for more WR production. Phillip Bell is next up in snaps, a 2025 4* who is involved but fairly pedestrian right now. Brock Boyd played early in the season but hasn't played since mid-October. He also wasn't on the injury list last week, but didn't play. LSU transfer Kyle Parker is a veteran who had a productive season a year ago but only has three catches on the season. Those are all the names to keep an eye on at this position, where it's very much "Jeremiah Smith and everybody else", followed by McCuin, followed by the real "everybody else".
[AFTER THE JUMP: players 'n clips]

The softness at WR means more tight ends on the field. Nate Roberts and Mason Williams are the top two, with a fairly even split of catches between them, 15 for the former and 14 for the latter. They're also similar size, both between 6'4 and 6'5 and in the 240 lb. range. And both are better as checkdown guys than receiving weapons who will burn you down the seam. Bennett Christian is close to a pure blocking TE at 6'6/255, with no catches on 165 snaps this season (Christian had five catches last year). Maxence LeBlanc and Hunter Welcing played earlier in the season but did not appear against Nebraska.
The offensive line has been reasonably stable, with some health-related musical chairs. Center Carson Hinzman is a good veteran, a very grown up version of the freshman who got his ass handed to him throughout the 2023 season. He's evolved into a commendable starting center who has started every game for Ohio State. Luke Montgomery is an equally solid guard, having started all but one game at LG this season. Gabe VanSickle has been the RG more often than not, though Jake Cook got the start against Nebraska after having filled in for Montgomery when he missed the Northwestern game. VanSickle and Cook are both fine, emblematic of a line where most players are straddling that 70 grade from PFF that puts you beneath star level in my grading and above cyan level.
At tackle, Phillip Daniels started the year on the right side but suffered an injury in Week 2. He missed the next four games and then returned for three more games, only to get hurt again against Oregon. Daniels missed the last two and his replacement against Nebraska was Ian Moore. A 2024 4*, Moore was playing on the left to begin the season before shifting to the right side when Daniels went down, while Austin Siereveld then moved from RG to LT. I wasn't a fan of Siereveld as a guard back in 2024 but he improved a lot in 2025 at tackle, so I was surprised in August when I heard he was back in guard at camp. Since moving to LT, Siereveld has been cromulent, though not as good as I thought he was last season. If we go off last week, OSU's line will be Siereveld - Montgomery - Hinzman - Cook - Moore, with Daniels injured and VanSickle as the 6th to rotate in when needed. We'll see if that holds on Saturday.

Quarterback Dilithium Rating (Scale: 1 [Navarre] to 10 [Denard]): Now we begin to turn our attention to Luke Fahey and his rushing ability. Fahey's sack-adjusted rushing numbers for this season are 22 caries for 89 yards, per PFF, a solid ~4 YPC number that doesn't pop up as a staple of the Ohio State offense but is something you have to keep an eye on. Taking advantage of a light box against Nebraska, Ohio State dialed up a QB draw that Fahey was able to turn into a first down:

And QB Power to pick up a first down on 4th & 2:

Fahey doesn't appear terribly fast, nor is he humongous at only 5'11 and 206, but he looks comfortable enough shouldering contact to get to his destination. Likewise, he is willing to scramble and can turn them into positive plays:

I'd put Fahey at a 5 on our scale. It's a piece of the arsenal and can net Ohio State a few yards on a well-called designed QB run or allow Fahey to extend drives if he can escape the pocket and run for a few yards. But he is not yet a dual threat in the sense that we think about and the physical tools don't appear overwhelming.
Dangerman: So I was having trouble with this one because there's no one who jumps out on this Ohio State team. After all, they're not known for skill talent. Wait, what's that? They still have Jeremiah Smith? Okay, we'll go with him. The introduction:

And this was before the Nebraska game, in which Smith racked up 165 receiving yards, compared to 45 by all other Buckeye wideouts. On the season, Smith has 1,482 receiving yards, first in the nation and 83rd all time in single season receiving yards. His 17 touchdowns also lead the nation, though he will come up short of getting to the DeVonta Smith/Michael Crabtree tier for power conference wideouts all time in receiving yards, partially because OSU won't play enough games as a non-playoff team (DeVonta Smith played 15 games) and partially because this isn't an Air Raid, whiz-bang passing attack like the one Crabtree was win. Oh well, he'll have to settle for PROBABLY BEING THE HEISMAN TROPHY WINNER ANYWAY.
As for the clips, it feels redundant because all of you know who Jeremiah Smith is. He brought in two touchdowns against Nebraska. Uno:

And dos:

There was also this TD in garbage time against Oregon:

The full season highlight reel:

I'm not sure what else there is to say about Jeremiah Smith at this point. He's unparalleled. The route-running. The hands. The speed. He's not quite the physical tank that Calvin Johnson was but at 6'4/223, Smith has plenty of size. Smith owns the the B1G record in career receiving yards and TDs. He should go #1 in the 2027 NFL Draft. Whether whichever sorry franchise has the top pick is smart enough to pick him over Drew Mestemaker remains to be seen, but Jeremiah Smith is the best player in college football this season.
HenneChart: Ohio State's season changed in an instant when Julian Sayin was injured against Indiana, thrusting Luke Fahey into the spotlight. Most would have expected Bryce Underwood's classmate Tavien St. Clair, a top-end 5* in his own right, to take the wheel but he was usurped by Fahey, who is a class younger and with a far less shiny recruiting profile. To the credit of Ryan Day, I think he probably chose the right QB because Fahey hasn't been a train wreck. That said, he's not a QB on the cusp of the NFL as a freshman, which is the bar that Buckeye Nation was hoping to get out of Sayin this season:

For a freshman QB, this was solid! There were some issues but I'm not ultra down on Fahey. I think his best throw of the game was probably the touchdown to Smith that I showed you in the prior section, but this one was good too:

If you look at some of the other games, you see this beautiful ball to Jeremiah Smith in the Oregon game:

And on this play you see Fahey improvising just long enough to roll out and find Isaiah West in the end zone for a touchdown:

That's the good for Fahey. He leans on Smith heavily but he's been generally able to get the ball to him and makes some quality throws along the way. There were issues though, as I'm not entirely sure how comfortable Fahey is at reading the full field apart from Jeremiah Smith. He seemed to show hesitation when placed in situations where the defense backed off and clogged the field with bodies, somewhat reminiscent to me of that game in September 2022 when Maryland dropped eight into coverage repeatedly and young JJ McCarthy spun his tires a little bit. Plays like this:

Nebraska drops eight, Fahey waits around, doesn't appear to feel confident in anything, bails and runs out of bounds short of the sticks. I marked that one down as a throwaway because he gained no yardage on the "scramble", one of three in the game, which is a fairly high number. I wouldn't be totally confident of all of Fahey's decisions yet, as he leans on Smith because he's a human cheat code but when sped up or facing a coverage he doesn't understand, some problems can arise. Northwestern threw a blitz at him and Fahey rushed, throwing a bad ball that was deflected and intercepted:

There are also some accuracy troubles. Fahey has McCuin open on a 4th & 2 against Oregon but puts the ball behind him:

It's a work in progress, as we'd expect with a quarterback of Fahey's age and experience. He's far from the worst case scenario you could have in a situation like this, even though there have been some very painful moments, as in the Oregon game when Ohio State's offense has dried up. I'm not sure if Fahey is Ohio State's QB of the Future and he's certainly not in the mold of Ohio State of yore, where the backup QB who came in when the starter got injured was sometimes JT Barrett, Cardale Jones, or Dwayne Haskins. But he's good enough to not submarine this offense, which is a good sign for a 3* true freshman.

Overview
Ohio State's offense comes into this game still sitting pretty. They have compiled 446.8 yards per game and 34.3 points per game, although their gaudy numbers contrast between halves of the season. If we look at the first six games, the Buckeyes scored 56, 23, 59, 42, 31, and 45 points. Since then, a period that begins with the Indiana game that saw Sayin get injured, Ohio State has scored 19, 18, 28, 28, and 28 points, and one of those 28 point games is a little generous, as the Buckeyes scored two garbage time TDs after they were getting blown out by Oregon.
If we look at these last five games, the points per game average drops to 24.2 points per game and their yards per game average drops to 378.8 yards per game. More interesting as it pertains to Ohio State's offensive numbers is when you divide their games into Jeremiah Smith Yards and Non-Jeremiah Smith Yards. By game:
Indiana: 8 targets, 68 yards (8.5 YPP) - 60 plays, 245 yards (4.1 YPP)
USC: 12 targets, 83 yards (6.9 YPP) - 69 plays, 381 yards (5.5 YPP)
Oregon: 10 targets, 133 yards (13.3 YPP) - 61 plays, 280 yards (4.6 YPP)
Northwestern: 17 targets, 117 yards (6.9 YPP) - 50 plays, 252 yards (5.0 YPP)
Nebraska: 9 targets, 165 yards (18.3 YPP) - 40 plays, 166 yards (4.2 YPP)
When they throw the ball towards Jeremiah Smith, those plays do far better than any other plays. Only against a Lincoln Riley defense was Ohio State able to top 5 YPP on plays that aren't throwing the ball to Jeremiah Smith. The rest of this offense looks fairly pedestrian but when they throw it to #4, it still looks like a 2021-22 era Ohio State offense.
The pedestrian nature of the offense outside of targeting the fire-breathing dragon at receiver is something I imagine many will chalk up to Fahey but I think is more nuanced. Even if we go back to the Iowa game before Sayin's injury, Smith accounted for 206 of Ohio State's 324 passing yards in that game. There are two realities that I think shouldn't go ignored apart from QB play. One of those is a rushing game that is only so-so. The Buckeyes put together solid rushing days against lesser defenses like Illinois, Maryland, and USC, but were at 3.7 YPC (sack adjusted) against Texas and Indiana and 4.0 YPC against Oregon and Nebraska, on decently low volume in the latter two.
The Nebraska game had intermittent moments of rushing success but the Buckeyes weren't able to pave their opposition in that contest. This was one of their best rushing plays in that game:

And I do think Bo Jackson is good! I gave him a star on the diagram because if you let him get outside, you could be in trouble:

Oregon lost the edge and it ended in six points:

Jackson isn't as much of a between the tackles bruiser but he's not short on power. The issue is whether the offensive line can create those big rush lanes. Against Nebraska, the answer was largely no:

A lot of plays were like that, some decent push up front behind the interior of the line (especially C Carson Hinzman and LG Luke Montgomery) but nothing explosive because they struggled to consistently get Jackson outside the tackles and climb to the linebackers or safeties inside the tackles. I did think this play was pretty fun:

But I wasn't blown away by the line play overall on the ground, which has been a theme with Ohio State offensive lines in the past. Against Michigan's defensive front, it would be a very bad sign if the Buckeyes are paving Michigan defensive line because the UM defense should be good enough to keep this ground game to 3-4 yards per carry, forcing more on the plate of the pass attack. The offensive line isn't spectacular, a lot of guys who are just "fine". Austin Siereveld, Hinzman, and Montgomery all seem draftable to me, but not 1st rounders I'm circling or clamoring to see in an NFL uniform.
In pass protection, it's a similar story. Ohio State has the #45 team pass block grade to PFF, which seems fair. They are generally able to give Fahey the time he needs, but sometimes this happens:

That's Siereveld the LT beaten clean on that sack. I was a big fan of Siereveld at LT last year compared to his guard days, but being moved back to tackle this season hasn't led to the same play I saw in 2025. He and RT Ian Moore aren't quite bulletproof tackles and blitzes can have success getting a free rusher into the backfield:

The other hard reality of the offense I wanted to talk about besides the run game was the reality of the receivers besides Jeremiah Smith. It'll be fascinating to watch next season, as I think there is hope for Chris Henry Jr. to be the next star OSU receiver but he hasn't made a splash this season besides some heroism in the Indiana game:

That game seemed like it would be a launching point for Henry's freshman season but nothing much followed and he played only eight forgettable snaps against the Huskers. The conveyor belt that spat out Terry McLaurin, Chris Olave, Garrett Wilson, JSN, Marvin Harrison Jr. Emeka Egbuka, and Carnell Tate in the span of ~7 years doesn't seem to have as clear of a future. Without the same stable of next man up recruits, OSU dipped into the portal and found Devin McCuin, who is fine:

McCuin is a perfectly reasonable receiver, it's just in the context of Ohio State's history on offense he looks like a total bum as a #2 WR. Everyone else besides McCuin just sort of exists. Smith has 1,482 yards, McCuin has 406 yards, Henry has 283 yards, and no one else has more than 2019 yards. That would be Nate Roberts, one of Ohio State's rather ho-hum tight ends. Roberts didn't record a catch against Nebraska but Mason Williams did, which gives you a feel for what these tight ends are capable of:

Sure, fine. Running backs feature a bit in the pass game, Jackson with 26 catches to make him the third most prolific on the team in terms of receptions and sometimes that can be useful to nerf a blitz:

Jackson is also a useful checkdown guy over the middle to allow Fahey to avoid sacks, serving as something close to the safety blanket that Brandon Inniss was supposed to be before injury plagued his season. Isaiah West has 13 catches of his own and it just occurred to me that we didn't mention West much. He's been forced into RB2 duty after the injury to Ja'Kobi Jackson back in October and has been alright, though with the two fumbles in the last two games holding him back. I would think OSU will ride Jackson hard on Saturday at the RB position. And that's about all I have for you today.

What does this mean for Michigan?
The current version of Ohio State's offense is a solid unit. I remember the Ryan Day-led offenses that were seemingly unstoppable terrors. That 2021 unit is the best collegiate offense I've ever scouted in my time doing this and probably the 2nd-best I've watched (2019 LSU). It had 3 future Pro Bowl caliber receiver including a Baby GOAT + TreVeyon Henderson + a future Pro Bowl QB + a good OL. It was absurd. This is a far, far cry from that.
The only piece on that level is Jeremiah Smith being JSN caliber. And I don't think Bo Jackson is far off from Henderson. Beyond that, it's a big drop off. Fahey is doing his job at an acceptable rate but is not an NFL QB yet. The other receivers besides Smith are eons away from Wilson/Olave. It's similar to the 2021 offense in that neither had great TEs (though Jeremy Ruckert was better than any of these guys) and their line isn't as strong as the 2021 unit (especially in pass protection). I view this 2026 group as a "good college offense" but not a great one. They are going up against, at the very least, a good college defense and probably a great one.
When we look at what Indiana and Oregon were able to do, I think a dialed in Michigan defense can have some success. Stripping away field position and any compromised situations that Michigan's inept offense may put the defense in, a similar outcome to what those two teams achieved feels doable (Indiana allowed 19 points, Oregon held OSU to 14 until it was prevent defense time). A really good defense should be able to keep the run game in check and limit what the other receivers can do while coaxing some mistakes out of Fahey either by mixing coverages or speeding him up through pressure. You won't throttle this group because Jermiah Smith is Him and you have to accept he's going to cook you some amount. But as long as it's not for the 200+ yards Iowa allowed, Michigan keeping Ohio State in check on offense is very much in play. It's just doubtful that'll be enough to win this game.

michigan.headline: Michigan Players Era Consolation Preview
michigan.body:
Instead of running away with the Players Era title with a trio of blowouts, the 2026-27 Michigan Wolverines are just trying to make it back home without complete humiliation. Tuesday’s demolition at the hands of Creighton was a bad omen, and now the Wolverines must find a way to salvage something from this tournament from the consolation side of the bracket.

Though hardware is always the goal, the good news is that opportunities remain to use this trip to help the resume. Even with a loss, the Miami Hurricanes are a good draw on Thanksgiving, as Michigan could use all of the Power Five wins it can acquire early on. Friday might bring another top-30 Kenpom opponent in the Alabama Crimson Tide, while the Kansas State Wildcats would create a must-win game as the alternative.

Honestly, there is not a ton to say following Tuesday. Mike Boynton’s squad is not playing well right now, which is spelling danger early for the head coach’s long-term viability. Though the calendar has not even hit December yet, the Wolverines will need to turn things around quickly if Boynton is going to last in this role. How the next two days go plays a non-trivial factor in that.

Thursday: vs. No. 17 Miami (3:30 p.m., ESPN2)

Given the holiday and quick turnarounds, I am not going into a ton of depth here, but will at least provide a little context heading into the final two games. Only Thursday’s opponent is known, as Miami also was upset in the opening round, falling to TCU. The Canes are 5-2 on the year, but all five losses have come against bottom feeders, while the only games against legitimate teams have ended in defeat.

Defense leads the way for Miami, though the metrics are skewed a bit by quality of competition. Florida hit 42 percent of its threes in the opener, while TCU made 39 percent of its attempts earlier this week. Michigan is really struggling in this area, down to 28 percent on the season, but against a physical interior, outside shooting is likely what provides the best chance to win.

On the other end, the Canes are equally as poor from deep (29 percent), but lean heaving into shots inside the arc. Miami gets to the rim, rebounds its misses, and does not turn the ball over ton. While its offense is not lethal, points will be hard to come by against its defense, meaning the Wolverines must be ready to defend the interior well, otherwise this will be a different-looking type of loss, but a loss all the same.

Friday: vs. No. 15 Alabama or Kansas State (5:30 p.m. or 8:30 p.m., ESPNU)

If the goal is simply stacking wins (which it might be for Boynton), then Kansas State would be the easier draw on Friday, but certainly Alabama provides the chance to earn the higher-quality win. The Crimson Tide lost close to Baylor on Thursday after a 5-0 start but still look like one of the 25 best teams in the country, which would actually set up decent stakes for a consolation final.

Alabama again features a fast-paced, efficient offense as Michigan saw in the Sweet Sixteen last season. Threes will always be a big feature of Nates Oats’ offense, and again few teams chuck up more than the Tide has this season. These attempts are currently falling at a decent 35-percent clip, and this is a concern for the Wolverines after the debacle against Creighton.

Meanwhile, Kansas State is just 3-3 on the season and sits outside the Kenpom top 100…but does have a win over Creighton? The Wildcats have adjusted offensive and defensive efficiencies outside the top 100 as well and aside from good foul prevention, there are not a lot of impressive components of this team. Michigan would be clear favorites in this one.

As seems to be the trend, Kansas State loves to take a ton of threes, but is not outstanding at making them. The Wildcats do move the ball around well and Brandon Rechsteiner has been good on high usage, though the Wolverines should feel ok matching up against this offense. Defensively, Kansas State does not appear to be anything special and surrenders a ton of looks from three while rebounding well, but the Michigan bigs should not feel intimidated.

msu.headline: We Have Come to the End
msu.body:
A wide shot of the exterior of SHI Stadium, the home field of the Rutgers Scarlet Knights, before an NCAA FBS football game in Piscataway, United States, on October 3, 2026. (Photo by Dan Squicciarini/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images

Well, TOC, here we are.  At the end of another difficult football season, in this situation:

Michigan State has to beat Rutgers, on the road (Saturday, 4:15 PM ET, Big Ten Network), to earn a tie for last place in the 18-team Big Ten Conference.  They will be tasked with doing so, perhaps without their first and second string quarterbacks, and numerous other key players on both sides of the ball.

This article gets published before the first required football availability report, which comes out later tonight, but MSU QB Alessio Milivojevic took a hard hit to his left side / left arm two games ago against Washington.  He was seen on the sideline Friday against Oregon wearing a substantial brace.  I have no idea what specific type of injury this would be supporting, but it just seems unlikely that it would heal up in time for Saturday.

On top of all this, the Spartans are coming off a 45-7 beatdown at the hands of Oregon while Rutgers is riding high after a 25-24 win over Penn State, their first in Happy Valley since 1988.

Ok, this is enough negativity for one article.  Let’s look for some positives.

While the Spartans’ record and standing in the Big Ten has not improved this year, things still feel different.  MSU has responded to bad losses early in the season to Nebraska and Wisconsin.  They’ve continued to play hard and came up just short to Illinois, Northwestern, and Washington.  Regardless of what happens on Saturday in New Jersey, the season will be most remembered for the win at Michigan, which showed the culture and style of play Pat Fitzgerald is trying to recreate at MSU.

However, it would still be nice to build off the UM win with something other than a close loss to Washington.  That will hopefully come via a solid transfer portal haul in January but a win at Rutgers certainly wouldn’t hurt MSU as they plan their portal possibilities.

In 2024, under Jonathan Smith, Michigan State had a nice 32-20 win against Iowa in mid-October and then a real chance to win at Michigan the following Saturday.  The Spartans blew that chance in Ann Arbor and then got blown out by Indiana and Illinois.  The season ended with a 41-14 home loss to Rutgers that kept the Spartans from bowl eligibility and was every bit as bad as the score would indicate.

Many might argue that the final nail in Smith’s coffin at MSU was the 2025 Homecoming loss to UCLA but perhaps it all started by failing to capitalize on that Iowa win two years ago.

I don’t know if the Spartans will win at Rutgers on Saturday but I also don’t see this season ending like it did in 2024.  Michigan State will, once again, come to play.  A victory might hinge on if third string quarterback Kayd Coffman can stay consistent, manage a whole game, and avoid turnovers.  We’ll look at keys to the game at the end but first, let’s take a closer look at how Rutgers compares to MSU.

Join the conversation!

Fewer ads

Create community posts

Comment on articles, community posts

Rec comments, community posts

Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android.

Rutgers Season Recap

Until Saturday’s win at Penn State, Rutgers’ only two victories were on September 25 against Howard, 58-7, and 37-30 at Maryland on October 17.

Comparing common opponents with MSU, Rutgers has lost at Northwestern (42-14), to Michigan (28-21), at Wisconsin (31-10), and to Nebraska (31-0).  Overall, Michigan State has fared slightly better against these teams.

Offensive Comparison

Rutgers may also have questions at quarterback coming into this game.  Boston College transfer Dylan Lonergan started the season but went out with a concussion in the October 24 loss at Northwestern and has not played since.  Lonergan was listed as questionable for the Penn State game but did not see the field.

The Knights stuck with junior signal called AJ Surace, who managed the game effectively against PSU.  He completed 24 of 39 passes for 178 yards, a touchdown, and no turnovers.  These numbers may not pop out but they’re not bad against a PSU defense that ranks first in the Big Ten in allowing just 151.5 yards per game through the air.  Surace also played well in the loss to Wisconsin, going 14-24 for 161 yards and a TD but struggled mightily against Northwestern, Michigan, and Nebraska.  Surace’s completion percentage in these three games was well under 50%.

For the season, Surace is completing 53.8% of his passes for 1025 yards on 6.5 yards per attempt, nine touchdowns, and seven interceptions.  Longergan is at 58.3% for 1066 yards on 8.3 yards per attempt, 10 TDs, and six picks.

Rutgers, however, like Michigan State, is a run-first team.  The Scarlett Knights have stuck to the ground on 56% of their plays this season but have managed just 3.8 yards per carry and 134.1 yards per game – good for 12th in the Big Ten.  For comparison, MSU is 16th with 106.5 yards per game on an abysmal 2.9 yards per carry.

Two primary backs lead Rutgers’ rushing attack.  Junior Antwan Raymond has gone for 911 yards and eight TDs on 4.9 yards per carry.  Sophomore Louisiana Tech transfer Clay Thevenin backs up with Raymond and has added 524 yards and five TDs on five YPC.

Overall on offense, Rutgers is 15th in the Big Ten with 23.4 points per game while MSU is dead last at just 17.7.  So, first team to three touchdowns has a good chance of winning this one.

Defensive Comparison

Rutgers seems to employ a base 4-2-5 defense and benefits from a pair of solid linebackers. Senior transfer from Drake Sean Allison and fellow senior Moses Walker anchor the middle of the Rutgers D and lead the team in tackles.

Overall though, Rutgers has struggled on defense in giving up 31.5 points per game this year, which ranks ahead of only Purdue in the Big Ten.  After giving up 45 to Oregon, Michigan State slipped a bit to 15th in the league at 25.3 PPG.

MSU’s D has been much better against the run in allowing 137.8 yards per game while Rutgers gives up 188.  With Jaziun Patterson returning to play against Oregon and Brandon Tullis finding some momentum in recent games, hopefully the Spartan run game can take advantage in this one and support whichever QB ends up under center for Michigan State.

The Spartan D, even if several key players remain out or limited by injury, should also provide an advantage in the pass game.  Rutgers gives up 223.2 yards per game in the air while Michigan State is tenth in the conference in allowing 206.5.  If Surace plays and MSU can just limit him to what he did at Penn State, then it could bode well for a Michigan State victory.

Keys to the Game for MSU

Penalties, Mistakes, and Near Misses.  After doing well to really limit penalties earlier in the season, they are starting to mount for MSU.  In their last four games, the Spartans had averaged 7.5 flags for 70 yards.  On top of the penalties, two key turnovers really hurt against Washington.  A muffed punt and other special teams errors made the Oregon game worse.  Finally, a couple of downfield passes that just missed against Washington hurt the Spartans’ efforts in that game.

The penalties might be a result of playing so many less-experienced backup players but, for all their efforts, this team just isn’t good enough to overcome so many mistakes.  Even though Rutgers has also experienced a tough season, Michigan State is going to need a clean game to win.

Quarterback Consistency.  Here, we’ll assume freshman Kayd Coffman gets his third start for MSU.  His first two have come against two of the Big Ten’s best teams in UCLA and Oregon.  It would be nice to see what Coffman can do against a team where MSU might be a little more evenly-matched.

At UCLA, Coffman completed his first four passes, with one going for a touchdown, as the Spartans took a 7-0 lead in that game.  Then, he went 0-6 with a crucial pick in Bruin territory before giving way to Leo Hannan.

Against the Ducks, Coffman missed on his first three attempts, then completed nine of his next 10, but went 1-6 with another interception the rest of the way before again giving way to Hannan.

Coffman maintaining a consistent output at Rutgers – say 15-23 for 170 yards, a TD, and no picks – and Patterson, Tullis, and the offensive line taking advantage of the Knights’ poor run defense to take some pressure off Coffman, could send the Spartans into portal season with a victory and some positive momentum.

Regardless of what happens Saturday, TOC, thanks for reading this previews.  Hopefully next year, we can look forward to them a little more.

msu.headline: Michigan State Film Room: A Duck Hunt Gone Horribly Wrong
msu.body:
EAST LANSING, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 20: The Michigan State Spartans offense lines up against the Oregon Ducks defense during the first half of a college football game at Spartan Stadium on November 20, 2026 in East Lansing, Michigan. The Oregon Ducks won the game 45-7. (Photo by Aaron J. Thornton/Getty Images) | Getty Images

For those of you who spent the weekend playing GTA 6 instead of watching Michigan State football, you didn’t miss much. If you stripped away the uniforms and logos on Friday night, you might have thought you were watching a MAC team collecting a paycheck against one of college football’s powerhouses. The talent disparity between Michigan State and Oregon was that glaring. In my opinion, this was the Spartans’ worst performance of the season, and the 45-7 final score was a fair reflection of what transpired on the field.

As I discussed in my recent article on NIL spending, the Ducks’ estimated football roster budget is more than double that of Michigan State. Oregon was bigger, faster, stronger and deeper than MSU, and it showed.

The Ducks more than doubled MSU in total offense (422 to 205 yards), averaged 4.9 yards per carry to MSU’s 2.3 and converted 67% of their third downs. Michigan State won the time of possession battle and got a solid performance from its punter, but beyond that, it was slim pickings for positives.

I wish there was more to highlight from this game, but everyone saw the bad, and we don’t need another Film Room pointing out the obvious.

This week, we’ll take a closer look at what young quarterback Kayd Coffman showed in his second collegiate start and a couple of encouraging plays from redshirt freshman running back Jace Clarizio. We’ll also examine Oregon’s fake field goal and why the overmatched Spartans should have been taking more chances on special teams.

Let’s dive into the film!

Kayd Coffman: A Trial by Fire

As I pointed out over the weekend, it’s hard to imagine a more daunting set of circumstances for a true freshman quarterback making his first two collegiate starts. Coffman drew No. 9 UCLA and No. 13 Oregon, two teams I believe could legitimately win a national championship this season. The College Football Playoff looks wide open without a clear-cut favorite.

I could easily see five players from Oregon’s defense alone being selected in the first three rounds of the 2027 NFL draft: defensive tackles A’Mauri Washington and Bear Alexander, edge defenders Matayo Uiagalelei and Teitum Tuioti, and safety Koi Perich. That’s a significant challenge for any quarterback, let alone a true freshman.

Coffman completed 10 of 19 passes for 106 yards with no touchdowns and one interception. He was sacked just once. Nothing about that stat line jumps off the page, but I thought Coffman held his own considering the caliber of competition he faced. For the most part, he avoided putting his team in difficult situations and, at times, displayed a level of composure well beyond his years.

Two plays against Oregon caught my attention and deserve a closer look.

PLAY 1: Coffman Baits the Ducks

Late in the first quarter, Michigan State appeared to have converted a 3rd-and-1, but an illegal shift penalty on tight end Kai Rios negated the first down. Instead of moving the chains, the Spartans found themselves facing a much more difficult 3rd-and-6 against an aggressive Oregon defensive front.

With the Ducks looking to pin their ears back and get after the quarterback, Kayd Coffman (No. 10) manufactures a free play. Using a savvy fake snap with his hands, likely accompanied by a hard count, Coffman draws Oregon outside linebacker Nasir Wyatt (No. 31) offside.

What I also love about this play is the awareness both Coffman and Fredrick Moore (No. 6) display in recognizing the flag and getting on the same page. Watch Moore at the bottom of the screen. He appears to adjust his original route, and the two essentially start playing backyard football, something I hope many of us will be doing this Thanksgiving. Throw the ball up in the vicinity of your receiver and give him an opportunity to come down with it.

There could have been a defensive holding penalty called on this play as well, but Moore still manages to make an incredible one-handed catch along the left sideline. The concentration, coordination and body control required to make that catch are exceptional. As spectacular as the catch was, don’t overlook the football IQ both players displayed.

PLAY 2: Losing the Moments That Matter

After picking up three yards on 3rd-and-6, Michigan State finds itself facing a manageable 4th-and-3 at the Oregon 28-yard line. I have no issue with the decision to go for it here, and I actually really like the play call. Unfortunately, this is another example of Michigan State failing to execute in a pivotal moment.

One of the biggest improvements I want to see from Michigan State next season is its ability to execute when it matters most. Watching the ESPN docuseries “Saban”, I was intrigued by the performance philosophy Nick Saban developed with the help of psychiatrist Dr. Lonny Rosen, nicknamed “The Wizard.” Football is a 60-minute game often decided by a handful of crucial moments, and far too often this season, the Spartans have lost those moments.

Michigan State lines up in a bunch formation with running back Kenneth Williams (No. 32) going in motion from left to right before running a wheel route. Bryson Williams (No. 14) appears to run a deep post route, while Chrishon McCray (No. 13), Samson Gash (No. 5) and tight end Carson Gulker (No. 12) run inbreaking routes designed to find the soft spots in Oregon’s zone coverage.

Credit to offensive coordinator Nick Sheridan for dialing up a good combination of zone-beater routes against this Oregon defense. I really like how the three receivers form a triangle in the middle of the field, stretching the underneath defenders horizontally and vertically while giving Coffman multiple passing options at or beyond the first-down marker.

The offensive line blocks this play up well, and Coffman has plenty of room to pick up the first down with his legs. Watch right tackle Rakeem Johnson (No. 55) recognize Coffman starting to scramble and put himself in position to potentially deliver a block downfield.

An accurate throw or a successful scramble likely moves the chains here. Instead, the turf monster gets Coffman, resulting in a three-yard loss and a turnover on downs. Did former michigan linebacker Devin Bush sneak into Spartan Stadium the night before the game and leave us another divot? Somebody might want to check the security footage.

Look at Coffman’s eyes at the end of this play. He’s looking around in disbelief. Good decision, good scheme, good blocking and multiple opportunities to convert. Instead of extending the drive and potentially putting a touchdown on the board, Michigan State walks away empty-handed. Just another painful missed opportunity in a season full of them.

Why Wasn’t This Us?

What pains me most about Oregon’s successful fake field goal is that it should have been Michigan State pulling tricks out of the playbook. When you’re as overmatched as the Spartans were on Friday night, stealing an extra possession or extending a drive through a trick play can help neutralize some of that talent disparity.

PLAY 3: Oregon’s Fake Field Goal

Oregon is leading 10-0 with just seven seconds remaining before halftime and no timeouts. Facing a 2nd-and-10, the Ducks line up for a 33-yard field goal, and Pat Fitzgerald even calls a timeout before the snap. Watch Oregon’s kicker Gage Hurych (No. 97), holder Bailey Ettridge (No. 39) and tight end Jamari Johnson (No. 9) on the left side.

This is a beautifully designed fake by Oregon. Ettridge takes the snap and flips it to Hurych, who races around the left edge. However, watch Johnson at the point of attack. He appears to grab Michigan State linebacker Dion Crawford (No. 18) and take him to the ground. To me, that’s a pretty obvious missed holding penalty.

I’d love to have a better angle of Nikai Martinez (No. 21) and Tre Bell (No. 3) rushing off the edge of the field goal formation. Both appear to sell out for the block, leaving the perimeter vulnerable. Given the game situation, I’d much rather see one of those defenders maintain outside leverage than have both aggressively pursue a blocked field goal. I don’t know their exact assignments, but I’d be curious to know who was responsible for outside containment.

The missed holding call doesn’t excuse what happens next. Cam Stodghill (No. 12) has an opportunity to stop Hurych, but the kicker is running like Derrick Henry, with Stodghill bouncing right off him! We’re talking about a placekicker here. Crawford deserves credit for recognizing the fake almost immediately and reacting to the ball, only to be taken out of the play by his own teammate.

What makes this play particularly frustrating is the game situation. If Michigan State tackles Hurych inbounds short of the end zone and the clock expires, Oregon doesn’t even get three points. Instead of heading into the locker room trailing 10-0, Michigan State suddenly finds itself down 17-0.

Despite a solid punting performance from Rhys Dakin, it was a rough night for special teams coordinator LeVar Woods and his unit between Oregon’s successful fake field goal and the muffed punt by Chrishon McCray. When you’re already at a significant disadvantage on offense and defense, you can’t afford to lose the special teams battle, too. I miss the creativity and calculated risks from the program that once gave us Little Giants and Mousetrap.

The Hometown Kid Shows Some Flashes

Coming into the season, Jace Clarizio was a name I frequently heard from Michigan State fans who were eager to see what the young running back could do. The East Lansing High School product was the consensus No. 1 running back prospect in Michigan in the 2025 recruiting class and a four-star recruit according to ESPN. Clarizio gave Spartan fans quite the scare when he flipped his commitment to Alabama on Nov. 26, 2024, only to flip back and sign with Michigan State eight days later on national signing day. His father, Craig Johnson, played for George Perles and was a member of the 1988 Rose Bowl championship team. Between his hometown roots and family ties to the program, Clarizio is an easy guy to root for.

Given his recruiting pedigree, I found it interesting that the redshirt freshman entered the season seemingly sixth on the running back depth chart behind Cam Edwards, Jaziun Patterson, Marvis Parrish, Kenneth Williams and Brandon Tullis.

With injuries thinning out Michigan State’s running back room, we’re finally getting an opportunity to see more of the local kid. Clarizio (No. 25) recorded all six of his touches on Michigan State’s final offensive possession against Oregon, finishing with five carries for 17 yards and one reception for 12 yards.

Let’s take a closer look at two of those plays and what the redshirt freshman brings to the Spartans’ offense.

PLAY 4: From the Flat to a First Down

Late in the fourth quarter, it’s time to get some of the young guys on the field. We have Pope Leo himself, Leo Hannan (No. 15), in at quarterback and Clarizio lined up behind the tight end, off the line of scrimmage to the right of the formation.

Michigan State lines up in a bunch formation, giving the Spartans additional bodies near the line of scrimmage to chip defenders or help with pass protection. Oregon has eight defenders in the box, all relatively close to the line of scrimmage, likely anticipating a run.

There’s no pre-snap motion, and Michigan State releases three pass catchers to the left and two to the right, stretching Oregon’s defense horizontally. Credit to Sheridan for dialing up a good play for a young quarterback against this defensive look. It’s a simple half-field read for Hannan, with Samson Gash running a curl route and Clarizio releasing into the flat.

Oregon brings an overload blitz to the right side of Michigan State’s offensive formation, sending outside linebacker Dutch Horisk (No. 41) and defensive back Aaron Scott Jr. (No. 14), who initially lined up across from Gash and Clarizio. Hannan makes the correct read and gets the ball out quickly, although Scott appears to get a fingertip on the pass with his long reach.

What I like about Clarizio here is his concentration in bringing in this wobbly duck. A lot of young players get excited when they see that much open space in front of them and start running before securing the football. Clarizio makes sure to complete the catch before turning upfield and going to work.

Once Clarizio turns upfield, he makes Oregon linebacker Cruz Rushing (No. 34) look like he just hit a patch of Michigan black ice. A quick change of direction leaves Rushing grasping at air. Clarizio turns a simple pass into the flat into a 12-yard gain, all coming after the catch. That ability to create yards on his own is something this offense has desperately needed.

PLAY 5: Making Plays in Space

As much as I liked what Clarizio showed on the previous play, I liked this one even better. On the very next snap, the redshirt freshman showcases a little more of his elusiveness on what ends up being Michigan State’s longest run of the night.

Facing a 1st-and-15, Michigan State runs a classic zone-read concept to the right side of the formation. Watch redshirt freshman wide receiver Charles Taplin (No. 19). He initially lines up on the right, motions left behind the line of scrimmage before reversing direction and coming back to the right to serve as a lead blocker for Clarizio.

Oregon lines up in a 4-3 defensive front with its linebackers playing close to the line of scrimmage, seemingly anticipating a run. At the snap, the linebackers follow their keys and flow toward the football. Oregon simply has more defenders than Michigan State has blockers on the play side, leaving Clarizio with very little room to operate.

Once again, Cruz Rushing finds out how difficult Clarizio is to tackle. Clarizio jukes Rushing out of his socks in the backfield before reversing direction and cutting back across the formation against the original design of the play. He puts another defender in the blender, forcing Anthony Jones Jr. (No. 28) to miss a tackle and turning what should have been a negative play into a 10-yard gain.

This run reminded me a little of Kenneth Walker III. Sometimes the numbers aren’t in your favor, and you need a running back who can improvise and make a little magic happen on his own. Love to see it!

It was also nice to see some different faces on the field during this final possession, including redshirt freshman Braylon Collier (No. 17) at wide receiver, Antonio Johnson (No. 54) and Rustin Young (No. 73) along the offensive line, and true freshman Eddie Whiting (No. 84) at tight end. As forgettable as this game was, there was at least some value in getting these young guys game experience against a talented Oregon defense.

Final Thoughts: Just Beat butgers

Despite the lopsided loss to Oregon, I came away encouraged by what I saw from Kayd Coffman and Jace Clarizio.

That being said, Michigan State absolutely has to beat Rutgers this week. We’ve spent enough time talking about player development and building toward the future. I want Pat Fitzgerald to put the players on the field who give Michigan State the best chance to win, regardless of age or class. Send the seniors out with a victory and give Spartan fans something positive to take into the offseason.

I’m curious to hear from Spartan fans. Who would you like to see start at quarterback against Rutgers? Go back to Alessio Milivojevic if he’s healthy, give Cam Fancher one last shot, stick with Kayd Coffman or hand the reins over to Leo Hannan? Who gives Michigan State the best chance to win? Let me know in the comments.

Bottom line: Beat butgers. Whatever it takes. Kick 12 field goals. Win 2-0 because the Rutgers punter accidentally steps out of the back of the end zone. Run the ball 90 times and let the quarterback finish with more handoffs than a Chick-fil-A drive-thru. Fake a punt on 1st down. I don’t care.

Just win the damn game.

If you haven’t checked it out already, here’s our latest game breakdown on The Red Cedar Rundown. We’re live Sundays on YouTube, so come hang out, give us a like and subscribe while you’re there.

You can also find me on X @W00dsyOwl. Thanks for your support!

msu.headline: Women’s Soccer Advances, Men Kicked Out
msu.body:
The NCAA Soccer Tournaments began this weekend with both the Michigan State Men’s and Women’s Teams hosting games.

The Spartans Women earned a #1 seed and faced 16th-seed Central Connecticut State on Saturday.  The game went the way a 1-vs.-16 game should go.  MSU won 7-0 to advance to the round of 32.  The Spartans had two goals each from Bella Najera, Kennedy Bell, and LJ Pearcy along with one from Lacey Kindel.  After leading 4-0 at the half, MSU got both their 2nd and 3rd string goalkeepers in after halftime.  None of the 3 goalies had to record a single save.

Here is the first Spartan goal, which proved to be the game winner.

Bella Najera scores her FOURTH goal of the postseason!  Sargeant and Briggs with the assists to give MSU a 1-0 lead. pic.twitter.com/xOTMEYdkRD
— Michigan State Women's Soccer (@MSU_wsoccer) November 21, 2026

MSU will host their round of 32 game as well.  That game will be this coming Friday, November 27, against Xavier.

The MSU Men also earned the right to play their first game at DeMartin Stadium as a 4-seed.  Unlike the women’s tournament with 64 teams, the men’s tourney only has 48 teams, so the top 4 seeds in each region get a bye to the round of 32.  MSU hosted Marshall today after the Thundering Herd took down Bowling Green on Thursday.

After 90 scoreless minutes, the game went to overtime.  There were no goals in the extra sessions either, so the game headed to penalty kicks.  Even as the higher seeded team and the home team, Marshall outperformed Michigan State for large portions of the game, winning the shots-on-goal battle, 8-5.  The Spartan goalie, Jake Grekowicz, made a couple of challenging saves in the overtimes that nearly ended the game.

In penalty kicks, Marshall was the first team up.  Both teams made their first two attempts.  In the third round, Marshall converted but MSU’s shot was saved.  Each team made their 4th attempt, so Marshall led 4-3 heading to the 5th with a chance to win with another successful PK.  Sadly, Grekowicz was unable to make a save and Marshall picked up the win.

Had MSU won, they would have hosted the round of 16 game as the 1-seed in the region, Akron, was knocked off by Wake Forest earlier in the day.  The season comes to an end for the Men’s Team.

The Lady Spartans move on.  Their 7-0 win was the second largest victory in the tournament’s opening round; Alabama beat Jackson State, 12-0!  Get ready to tune in to that game on Friday to root on the Green & White as they look to advance to the 3rd round.

msu.headline: El Niño hits Spartans in The Weather Report
msu.body:
EAST LANSING, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 20: Dylan Raiola #8 of the Oregon Ducks celebrates his teammates second half touchdown run against the Michigan State Spartans at Spartan Stadium on November 20, 2026 in East Lansing, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Lots going on in the world of MSU sports this weekend. So, we thought let’s have some weather report fun and incorporate basketball, hockey and football all into this week’s report. Football was an ugly blood bath that we all saw coming. Hockey pulls off a split but had its own blood bath brawl in Yost. Basketball saw some solid bench action but the post is not looking good with the center position. Fellow TOC writer O helped out with this report and the basketball sun and cloud are coming from him. Without further adieu let us step into some sunshine.

Sun #1

My first sun is for the Spartan football team and coaches. They lost 45-7 you say, how could you possibly award the team a sun? This team has looked bad, and have had some very ugly games. This team has also had injuries that have superceded the last two years and those years were bad. What has changed this year is character. The team has character and fight. They are giving their best and not giving up. The number of underclassmen getting playing time, the number of athletes that are not the four stars Oregon is sending out there are all getting strong character development in Spartan grit. Fitz has the team playing. I’d be interested to see if he can get better athletes and take a good look at conditioning and what is going on with all these injuries. I know there is one more game but next year will really be the year to see what Fitz can actually potentially do.

Sun #2

Sun two brings us to the ice. MSU hockey has been off to a tough start and has been disappointing. Struggling to find their chemistry and identity with all the youth and lacking a true leader. Well, this weekend against the weasels MSU had an opportunity to perhaps turn the season in the right direction. Friday was an ugly game where the Spartans were manhandled and it all started with an early power play that had MSU behind practically from the start. Then we get to the melee. The hip check that the weasels felt very offended by. Barnhill and Vansaghi may have fought life back into this team. Even with both players suspended for game two and into the OSU series, they maybe let out frustrations of an entire team in an early season. Saturday night, an entirely different MSU team took the ice. Down defenders, Ward and Jurecki brought energy and the sticks were active Saturday. MSU out shot, out played, and out scored the number one team in the country. They looked like the team we have been waiting for. Yes, the weasels were short forwards, but MSU was down defenders. Ravensbergen looked outstanding, except when he left his post open, but still had the shut out. This might be a breath of fresh air that they needed to get into the winning column. The team is talented, now let’s continue to play like it.

Sun #3

Our basketball sun is going to Kur Teng. Teng had a career high 24 points on 8/11, and 5/8 from 3. Teng showed he can be a reliable shooter for this team. This allows the team to not rely on Scott and Jervis and sometimes Fears for all the perimeter shooting. Teng has always been smooth from three but has never been consistent or had a break out performance. Hopefully Teng can get hot and be a weapon that draws coverage which can perhaps open up some paint play if the MSU big men can handle it.

Cloud #1

Football cloud goes to the teams health. MSU was doubled in yardage, had two turnovers, were terrible on third down and I’m still giving the cloud to health. The injuries on this team need to be figured out. Injuries have haunted this team for a few years now. So, what’s going on? Is there something going on in conditioning or practices? Is it dietary? Is it really just bad luck? Conditioning coaches have changed and we still have the problem. This year though, was unbearable. The injuries were so much it had to be difficult to game plan when you don’t end up having the players you need on the field. It is nearly impossible to be competitive against an Oregon with third string players and a freshman QB.

Cloud #2

As much as the brawl helped inspire my hockey sun, that same brawl inspires my hockey cloud. Losing Barnhill and Vansaghi for one game is bad enough. The reprucussions of suspensions could be greater and have implications down the road. Having a significant penalty means the two are going to have to stay out of trouble or a worse suspension will come their way. That is a tough ask for a player like Vansaghi who is the agitator  for MSU. He is the guy that comes to the defense of his teammates and will throw a punch at anyone. To have him have to change his way of play could be a learning process. In a team that needs a bit more leadership, Vansaghi is a guy that can provide that, the chip on the shoulder, and the aggression. MSU needs him, so the suspensions will be something to keep an eye on.

Cloud #3

Our basketball cloud has been hinted at some but we can officially say it now goes to the centers. Taylor, McCulloch and Bonke had three combined field goals. They had six turnovers. None of them can be relied upon to be fed the ball in the low post and make a move to beat a defender. They are only scoring on rebounded put backs or a wide open Fears feed. To make things worse, the coaching staff didn’t even try to run any of those sort of plays. Bonke has been disappointing all season and Taylor is still developing. Regardless, the Spartans need a lot more production from the big guys in the paint. MSU typically struggles at the arc but has had some success there this season. If they can get stronger in the block and stay hot outside, they will be very difficult to beat. Hopefully, they can work out these kinks before the schedule gets even tougher in B1G play.

There we have it. As a big follower and fan of MSU hockey, I was very happy to see this team look like itself and take down number 1 at Munn. That was my favorite moment of the weekend. The lineup changes may be the key to staying hot on the ice. As always, I look forward to seeing where your clouds and suns lie in the comments. I wish you all a Happy Thanksgiving and be thankful there’s only Rutgers left on the football schedule. Go Green!
