tigers.headline: Tigers to sign RHP Kevin Gausman to one-year deal, per report
tigers.body:
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 23: Kevin Gausman #12 of the Chicago Cubs celebrates during the fifth inning against the Miami Marlins at Wrigley Field on September 23, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Scott Harris and Jeff Greenberg continue to pile up major league free agent signings. On Wednesday evening, Jeff Passan of ESPN reported that the Detroit Tigers are in agreement with veteran right-handed starting pitcher Kevin Gausman on a one-year deal worth $25 million. The deal is pending a physical.

The 35-year-old Gausman has been one of the more durable and effective starters in baseball over the last decade. He’s topped 170 innings in each of the last six seasons, pitching in 2020-2021 for the San Francisco Giants, where Scott Harris was the GM at the time, and then the Toronto Blue Jays from 2022-2026. The Jays traded him to the Chicago Cubs at the 2026 trade deadline, where he finished the season.

Gausman will mix in his slider occasionally, but he’s essentially a two-pitch pitcher, utilizing his fourseam fastball and outstanding splitter almost exclusively. He used the fourseamer 50.6 percent of the time in 2026, averaging 93.8 mph with above average extension. It’s not quite the bat misser it was when Gausman threw a little harder, but his command and good life on the pitch have continued to make it an effective fastball. His splitter continues to rack up a huge amount of swing and miss, with hitters whiffing 42.9 percent of the time in 2026.

Gausman struck out 24.5 percent of hitters faced last season, with his customary low walk rate of 6.3 percent. He’s typically suppressed home runs quite well, especially in the last half decade, but he did finally have a couple of rough outings with the Cubs in which he gave up more homers than usual. Transitioning to a new team with new catchers, in a ballpark that can be favorable to the long ball in the summertime, probably explains all of it. Gausman is still an above average starting pitcher, and we’re not going to put too much into his rough two months in Chicago. However, his 4.51 ERA was his worst, and the first time he’s been over 4.00, since 2019.

Adding Gausman is probably an upgrade to the Tigers’ starting rotation. Framber Valdez, Gausman, and after signing a long-term deal, Troy Melton can all be inked into the Opening Day rotation. That would leave Jackson Jobe, Keider Montero, Luis Gil, River Ryan, Drew Anderson, Reese Olson, and Andrew Sears theoretically vying for the final two spots in the rotation. That’s quite a lot of pitching depth, and assuming the injuries are at a normal level next year, should allow them to flex a few of those pitchers into the bullpen.

Where this is hard to process, is in the fact that by building in all this depth with major league signings, the Tigers risk pushing some optionable pitchers off the 40-man roster. If everything works out, they’ll have so much pitching it shouldn’t matter, but if some of these pitchers don’t perform as hoped, and there are always at least a few, they’re going to clog up the 26-man roster to a degree. That’s probably a risk worth taking, because pitchers like River Ryan and Olson, if he’s finally healthy, aren’t built up to throw a starter’s workload anyway, but the roster crunch is going to be real if spring camp concludes with most of these pitchers healthy. Of course, at that point teams are desperate for pitching, and the Tigers might even have an opportunity to trade from a deeply stacked hand.

Gausman’s 2026 numbers lend themselves to a little concern that he may be tipping into a real decline phase, but his stuff, his strikeout and walk rates, and his contact data all look normal. He certainly adds veteran presence and a long, long track record of consistent good performance to the Tigers’ starting rotation. It feels like overkill to a degree, with the Tigers still not exactly stocked with high leverage relief options even after adding Emilio Pagán, but the uncertain medical status of players like Olson and Will Vest has to be factored into the equation as well. They’ve been rumored to have interest in RHP Bryan Abreu, the top right-handed reliever left in free agency, but my guess would be this puts an end to that speculation.

The Tigers will need to DFA two pitchers to open spots for Gil and Gausman, as well as a position player to make room for Ha-Seong Kim. There are only so many major league pitching signings you can make before you’re pushing useful, and just as importantly, optionable pitchers off the 40-man roster. Still, as long as the additions are upgrades, it’s hard to go wrong. If the Tigers manage their staff well and move the right starting pitchers to the bullpen, they should be pretty strong in both the rotation and the bullpen.

Right-hander Kevin Gausman and the Detroit Tigers are in agreement on a one-year, $25 million contract, pending physical, sources tell ESPN. Gausman, 35, is one of the best workhorses in baseball, with the second-most innings of any pitcher since 2021.
— Jeff Passan (@JeffPassan) November 25, 2026

tigers.headline: Get to know your Tigers Rookies of the Year
tigers.body:
Tigers great Lou Whitaker was introduced during a ceremony to retire Whitaker's No. 1 before the game against the Rays on Saturday, Aug. 6, 2022, at Comerica Park. Tigers2 | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

We were all thrilled around here when the 2026 American League Rookie of the Year award went to Tigers infielder Kevin McGonigle. He was certainly a worthy candidate: he led the American League in WAR (according to Baseball Reference), which is mighty impressive. But did you know he also led the league in plate appearances? Nobody in the league came to the plate more often than McGonigle, which shows you just how reliable and durable he was as a centerpiece of the Tigers’ lineup.

Five other Detroit Tigers have won the Rookie of the Year award, which began in 1947; for the first two years there was only one awarded across Major League Baseball, with individual leagues giving out their awards in 1949. That doesn’t seem like too many, and perhaps it isn’t, but I think you’ll agree some of the Tigers who have won these awards have been pretty special players. (All WAR values are bWAR, because I love Baseball Reference

#1: Harvey Kuenn (1953)

Rookie WAR: 1.7

Career WAR: 25.8 (15 seasons)

Career batting average/OPS/OPS+: .303/.765/108

Kuenn (pronounced “keen”) was from Wisconsin, attended the University of Wisconsin, and later went on to manage the Milwaukee Brewers to their only previous American League pennant (although they fell to the Cardinals in the 1982 World Series). But he made his mark in Michigan on some pretty terrible Tigers teams of the 1950s, after foregoing his final year of college eligibility in 1952 to briefly play in the Tigers’ minor-league system before permanently becoming a major-leaguer in September of that year.

Like McGonigle, Kuenn led the American League in plate appearances. He also led the league in hits, and in 731 plate appearances he struck out a scant 31 times. He would never strike out 40 times in a season, which is totally bonkers by today’s standards. Kuenn easily beat Boston’s Tom Umphlett for the Rookie of the Year award; Umphlett would have two more forgettable years in Washington and then spend another decade in the minor leagues.

While Kuenn didn’t hit many home runs — his career-high was a dozen in 1956 — he could certainly hit line drives for doubles, leading the American League in two-baggers three times. In 1958 he moved to the outfield and would occasionally play third base as well. He was also involved in one of the most famous trades in baseball history: just before the 1960 season, after leading the American League with a .353 batting average in 1959, he was traded to Cleveland for Rocky Colavito, who’d led the league in home runs with 49 in ‘59. Can you imagine that trade?! Holy moly.

After a year in Cleveland he spent several seasons with the Giants, Cubs and Phillies, mostly playing in the outfield but transitioning to primarily pinch-hitting by the end of his career in 1966. He was the Brewers’ hitting coach for most of the 1970s, and became their manager for two seasons in the early 1980s. He was plagued by heart and circulation issues, and had part of a leg amputated before he turned 50, dying of a heart attack before 60.

#2: Mark Fidrych (1976)

Rookie WAR: 9.6

Career WAR: 11.4 (5 seasons)

Career ERA/ERA+: 3.10/126

What can you say about Fidrych that hasn’t already been said? He was, at the same time, both larger than life and completely down to Earth. His flame burned white-hot for one season, and then an injury took him down immediately after and he never recovered. What could he have done in a full career? Would he have been one of the all-time greats, or another Joe Charboneau? Nobody knows.

In the Appalachian League in 1974, the lanky Fidrych had quite the head of curly hair; his manager thought he looked a bit like a bird, and the nickname stuck. In 1976 he started the season in the bullpen, being used sparingly before moving into the rotation. He completed 24 (!!) of his 29 starts, throwing four shutouts along the way. The famous “Yankees Game” saw him go the distance on national television; if you have never watched that game, my goodness, take the next two-plus hours and do just that. It is incredible and delightful and amazing for a boatload of reasons.

(Did you know Rusty Staub was afraid of flying, and was a gourmet cook? The announcers mentioned that seconds before a fly ball caught the right-field overhang at Tiger Stadium.)

If you don’t have two-plus hours to spare, skip to the ninth inning in the video. The Stadium is going nuts, Fidrych is clearly way too hyped-up but he closes it out with a grounder to second, and after the final out he shakes the hands of his teammates, umpires, the grounds crew, fans, and probably a police officer. He’s barely old enough to legally order a beer, and almost fifty thousand people chanted his name to get him out on the field to tip his cap. You can watch a lot of baseball games and never see anything quite like that.

Did the massive workload take a toll on Fidrych’s body? Probably, but in the ‘70s it wasn’t unheard-of for a pitcher to finish more than half of his starts. (Mind you, plenty of pitchers suffered career-ending injuries because of it; the Nolan Ryans and Mickey Loliches of the world were the exceptions.) He hurt his knee in spring training the following year, but came back in May and was as dominant as he’d been the year before. But in July he felt something go wrong in his arm, and tried to pitch through it but he was never the same. As it turns out, he tore his rotator cuff — a serious but hardly career-ending ailment these days — and his career ended in 1980.

Fidrych went back to his native Massachusetts and lived a quiet life: he drove a truck and bought a farm, marrying and having a daughter. Sadly, like Kuenn before him, he would die much too young: in 2009 he was working underneath a truck, which fell and killed him. (I was at a Tigers game that day with my brother, and we heard the news during dinner at Gar’s Bar in Marine City, Michigan. I don’t believe I was able to finish my Garburger.)

#3: Lou Whitaker (1978)

Rookie WAR: 3.8

Career WAR: 75.1 (19 seasons)

Career batting average/OPS/OPS+: .286/.789/117

As long as Whitaker is not in the Baseball Hall of Fame, I will not set one foot in Cooperstown, New York.

Drafted out of high school in Virginia, he started off as a third baseman in the minor leagues, but switched to second base in 1977 while playing at Double-A Montgomery alongside a shortstop you may know. Famously, both he and the shortstop were called up to the Tigers on the same day, making their major-league debuts in the second game of a doubleheader at Fenway Park on Friday, September 9, 1977.

Neither he nor the shortstop hit too many home runs in 1978: Whitaker had three of the total five between the pair. But both of them would find power within a few years, Whitaker topping twenty home runs four times in an era in which that was an unusual feat for a middle infielder. Early in his career, defence was Whitaker’s calling card, and in his rookie year that was undeniably true: his Range Factor per 9 innings was tops in the American League, and it would be above the league average every year for the first five years of his career.

If you were a Tiger fan in the 1980s, it was easy to take Whitaker and the shortstop for granted. They were just there, day after day, being extremely good baseball players. Getting on base, hitting some home runs, and turning more double plays than any other pair of teammates in history. I doubt that record will ever be broken: can you imagine two teammates playing side-by-side for nineteen straight seasons, almost every day, at two crucial defensive positions?

The question about Whitaker has always been, was he merely “good” and not “great” as one might expect from a Hall of Famer? I know WAR is a counting statistic (and there are things you can say about such things), but the fact that the only six second basemen above him in career WAR are in the Hall of Fame — and another fourteen below him in career WAR are in there as well — needs to count for something. You need to be durable, consistent, and more than anything else, very very good at what you do, to put up cumulative numbers like that.

I’m biased, of course: I want Whitaker to be in the Hall of Fame, right beside the shortstop. It would’ve been great if they’d been inducted at the same time, but that did not happen. The shortstop went on at length about how Whitaker belonged there in his acceptance speech, as he should have. Your move, Cooperstown.

#4: Justin Verlander (2006)

Rookie WAR: 4.0

Career WAR: 82.3 (21 seasons)

Career ERA/ERA+: 3.33/128

For those of you who have been living under either a rock or some other heavy object for the past couple of decades, Verlander was a pitcher who was very good for a very long time who retired after the 2026 season, rejoining the Tigers for one last go-round after being with them from 2005 to the midpoint of the 2017 season.

Verlander was drafted in 2004, the second pick overall out of Old Dominion University in Virginia. (Matt Bush was first overall that year; he took a circuitous route to the Major Leagues, to put it bluntly.) He started the 2005 season in High-A Lakeland, mowing down hitters with ruthless efficiency before being promoted to Double-A Erie where he did the same thing. He made two starts with Detroit that season, but those didn’t go so well. Thankfully that wouldn’t be the case the following year when he came north with the Tigers out of Spring Training and didn’t look back.

The 2006 season was pure magic for Tigers fans, and Verlander’s role on that team was a significant one. He made 30 starts, went 17-9, and easily won the Rookie of the Year award over second-place finisher Jonathan Papelbon. (Four other people receiving votes in either league ended up playing for the Tigers at some point: Francisco Liriano, Ian Kinsler, Anibal Sánchez and Prince Fielder. Neat)

You probably know the rest of his story: three Cy Young awards, a league MVP, some no-hitters, the deadline trade to Houston and the subsequent World Series rings which stung more than a little. (He also finished second in the Cy Young voting three times.) He’s as much of a lock to go into the Hall of Fame on the first ballot; the only question in my mind is, will he be the second-ever unanimous pick, or will Miguel Cabrera beat him to that? His 266 career wins might just be the highest total we see in a pitcher from here on out.

The Tigers signed him to pitch for the 2026 season, and he was injured in his first start of the year in Arizona after three innings. He worked hard all season, despite some setbacks, to pitch one last time — which he did on the season’s penultimate day, against the Pirates. He acquitted himself well, pitching into the sixth and only allowing two runs on the day. Weird fact: the only two times he pitched that season were against National League teams. I still hate interleague play (but I loved watching American League pitchers bat).

#5: Michael Fulmer (2016)

Rookie WAR: 5.4

Career WAR: 12.8 (9 seasons so far)

Career ERA/ERA+: 3.93/110

This one is still a work in progress, as Fulmer is still pitching — when he can stay healthy, that is.

Originally drafted by the New York Mets, he came to the Tigers as a minor-leaguer in the trade that sent the mercurial Yoenis Céspedes away. Like Fidrych, Fulmer has been through injury troubles for most of his major-league career; unlike Fidrych, there are now surgeries and techniques that could have easily fixed Fidrych’s problems.

His rookie season in Detroit came at a strange time for the franchise; the core group of players that saw so much success in the first half of the decade was starting to fray and age, but could Fulmer lead a youthful resurgence to return the team to the top of the league again? (No, as it turns out.) He did well, though: an 11-7 record in 26 starts, keeping the ball in the yard for the most part. Like others of his generation, he didn’t really start finding his strikeout groove until a couple of years in the Majors, but he generally kept the Tigers in the game.

Alas, the all-too-common Tommy John surgery was performed in 2019 after feeling something in a Spring Training game, and he missed all of that season before some short, unsuccessful starts in the abbreviated 2020 campaign. He saw quite a bit of success in the bullpen in 2021 and 2022; at the trade deadline in 2022 he was dealt to the Twins in exchange for Sawyer Gipson-Long. He spent 2023 with the Cubs before needing more elbow surgery, taking him out for the following season.

In 2025 he pitched once for the Red Sox before rejoining the Cubs, and he split the 2026 season between the Angels and the Yankees. I’d say he’s now successfully reached “journeyman” status, but you have to wonder how long his arm can hold up before it breaks again. Who knows? He might pitch into his late 40s, doing a pretty credible Jamie Moyer impersonation.

How will we summarize McGonigle’s career when it’s all over? It’s impossible to predict, but by all meaningful measures he seems to be set up for long-term success so long as he stays healthy. I hope we can look back on his career and say phrases like “realized potential” and “sure-thing Hall of Famer;” time will tell, though.

tigers.headline: Detroit Tigers News: Kevin McGonigle, Troy Melton, Ha-Seong Kim, Tarik Skubal, free agency, CBA negotiations
tigers.body:
ATLANTA, GA - OCTOBER 06: Ha-Seong Kim #7 of the Atlanta Braves high fives his teammates before Game Three of the Division Series between the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Atlanta Braves at Truist Park on October 6, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Kevin D. Liles/Atlanta Braves/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Happy Wednesday, everyone! The free agent market has gotten hot this week, with teams and players looking to make deals before the potential lockout next week. CBA negotiations are now on pause for the Thanksgiving holiday, but we’ll be keeping a close eye on how those develop over the coming days. We also look at the Tigers’ move to sign infielder Ha-Seong Kim, the breakdown of the Troy Melton extension, and which teams didn’t make the cut on Tarik Skubal.

Let’s jump right into it!

Detroit Tigers News

The Tigers actually did something.

tigers.headline: Tigers sign SS Ha-Seong Kim to a one-year deal, per report
tigers.body:
ATLANTA, GA - OCTOBER 07: Atlanta shortstop Ha-Seong Kim (7) takes batting practice prior to the start of the NLDS game 4 between the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Atlanta Braves on October 7th, 2026 at Truist Park in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

At Troy Melton’s extension press conference on Tuesday morning, Scott Harris hinted that a move to shore up their infield defense was already in the works. It didn’t take long, as Jeff Passan of ESPN reports that the Tigers are in agreement with free agent shortstop Ha-Seong Kim on a one-year deal worth $5 million. Mark Feinsand of MLB.com reports that the deal includes another million dollars in performance bonuses that can be earned.

The Tigers have been linked to the 31-year-old infielder in previous offseasons, but nothing ever emerged. Kim has dealt with a litany of injuries in recent years, leaving the memory of his strong 2023-2024 campaigns with the San Diego Padres a bit distant. Kim had labrum issues with attendant inflammation in his right shoulder, his throwing arm, in late 2024 and 2025 that really limited him. He had surgery on the shoulder after the 2024 season and missed much of the 2025 season recovering.

He signed a one-year deal with the Braves last offseason, but a tendon injury to his right middle finger after a slip and fall on ice in his native South Korea required surgery and sent him repeatedly back to the injured list through the year. He appeared in just 51 games and couldn’t swing the bat at all, hitting just .116 on the year. The injury also affected his throwing and it was just a disaster of a season all around.

Scott Harris loves a cheap bet on a player to rebound from injury, and this is another example. Those bets have been failures. The recent signing of right-hander Luis Gil is another example of a deal where the risk is low and the reward fairly high, but the odds are pretty poor of it working out as hoped. Cumulatively, they’ve flushed a lot of money down the drain this way with nothing to show for it while avoiding obvious upgrades that would’ve required a more significant investment.

Kim was a star for the Kiwoom Heroes in the KBO for a few years before coming stateside. He signed a four-year deal worth $28 million with the San Diego Padres during the 2020-2021 offseason. He started off slowly in 2021, but from 2022-2024 was a consistent 3-4 WAR sort of player with excellent defense and roughly league average production at the plate.

After so much trouble with his shoulder, it’s not at all clear the Tigers will even get the defensive portion of Kim’s former abilities here. The finger injury at least seems like something that a long period of rest would have resolved. Labrum issues in your throwing arm are a lot more serious, though at least there was no reported trouble with the shoulder during his attempts to get back into form last year.

This is a small enough deal to just dump if John Peck cleans up his defense a little more and looks more capable of playing an above average shortstop. The problem is actually being willing to cut your losses quickly, which is something Harris has struggled with. There’s at least the chance that with all this time off, Kim will finally be well beyond the shoulder problems and ready to start getting back to his old form.

It’s a small bet on that possibility, but one would hate to see Peck have a strong spring camp only to get sidelined again while the Tigers run another low cost experiment. It’s also odd to make a move like this and not insist on a club option for 2028 in case it works out. Hard to believe many teams were clamoring for a player who arguably should be getting a minor league deal with an invite to spring camp Essentially, this is just a depth move, and so how they handle that competition for playing time, and how long they stick with Kim if he can’t get it going at the plate, is the crux of the issue.

tigers.headline: Teruaki Sato signs with Cubs, Freddy Peralta heads to Baltimore, and the Troy Melton extension is official
tigers.body:
TORONTO, ON - SEPTEMBER 14: Troy Melton #52 of the Detroit Tigers pitches during a game against the Toronto Blue Jays at Rogers Centre on September 14, 2026 in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. (Photo by Vaughn Ridley/Getty Images) | Getty Images

With the biggest of all free agents this offseason signed as Tarik Skubal agreed to a monster deal worth $450 million, the other big names are starting to come off the board in a hurry with a week left until owners lock out the players.

On Tuesday morning. longtime Hanshin Tigers star utilityman and slugger Teruaki Sato reportedly agreed to a six-year deal worth $120 million. The 2025 Nippon Professional Baseball MVP, who won the Triple Crown in 2026, joins an already potent Cubs positional group.

Not long after that deal dropped, right-hander Freddy Peralta was reported to have agree with the Baltimore Orioles on a five-year deal totaling $125 million. The former Milwaukee Brewers starter was traded to the New York Mets last offseason before his final year of team control. It went quite poorly, but after Peralta was traded to the Tampa Bay Rays at the trade deadline he was able to turn things around somewhat. While never an ace, the 30-year-old was a generally durable frontline starter for the Brewers. Even so, that’s a pretty big contract for a pitcher whose current projections look decidedly more like a fairly average mid-rotation arm.

The Cleveland Guardians also got into the mix a bit, signing longtime Royals left-hander Kris Bubic to a one-year contract worth $17.5 million. He’s been a good but oft-injured starting pitcher in Kansas City for most of his career. Since his 2023 Tommy John surgery, he’s had myriad rotator cuff and forearm issues that continue to limit his workload. Joining Cleveland’s vaunted pitching program will likely make him a bigger problem for the AL Central, but only if he finally puts the injuries behind him. That seems unlikely, but it’s a solid low risk speculative signing of the sort the Guardians prefer.

On Tuesday, the Tigers officially announced Troy Melton’s six-year extension which guarantees him $46.5 million with incentives, bonuses, and a club option that could make it a seven-year deal worth $80 million in total.

The Tigers officially announcing the Melton extension. pic.twitter.com/2YGpbMX828
— Rogelio C (@therogcast) November 24, 2026

There are still some big names out there in free agency. Top reliever Adrian Morejon, and outfielders Seiya Suzuki and Randy Arozarena are still available. As Sato plays some right field as well as third base, it will be interesting to see if the Cubs circle back to Suzuki at this point, but it seems much more likely that they’re out of the market for the 32-year-old.

Overall, free agency is moving very quickly and just about all the big names seem set on getting deals done before the lockout. Whether that signals a belief in the owners getting a salary cap in place, or whether Skubal’s massive contract and the flurry of signings means that players are trying to avoid the waiting game and uncertainly of a potentially long lockout is still anyone’s guess. With the Tigers still in need of some upgrades in the bullpen and perhaps the infield, we’ll see if Scott Harris has anything else to come, or whether at this point they think it better to let the CBA play out and see if the new payroll structure in the next CBA creates some opportunities.

tigers.headline: Tigers sign right-hander Luis Gil to a one-year deal, per report
tigers.body:
Apr 26, 2026; Houston, Texas, USA; New York Yankees starting pitcher Luis Gil (81) delivers a pitch during the second inning against the Houston Astros at Daikin Park. Mandatory Credit: Troy Taormina-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

The Detroit Tigers made another minor move on Sunday to shore up their pitching depth. Jeff Passan reports that the Tigers have signed RHP Luis Gil to a one-year deal worth $2.3 million, with a potential two million more in incentives. The deal is still pending a physical. Gil was non-tendered by the New York Yankees on Friday after a rough season on the mound for the 28-year-old veteran.

Gil’s career has already been a pretty wild ride despite his relative youth. The six-foot-three, 215 pound right-hander was initially signed as an international free agent out of the Dominican Republic as a teenager by the Minnesota Twins. In 2018, the Twins dealt him to the Yankees for outfielder Jake Cave. Gil developed into an excellent prospect in the Yankees’ system with eye-popping strikeout numbers, and eventually made his major league debut in 2021. The next season he blew out his elbow and required Tommy John surgery. He returned in 2024 and put together a strong campaign that earned him the AL Rookie of the Year award. A lat strain in 2025 and back issues in 2026 have limited him in the interim to just 84.1 innings over the last two seasons.

There are some reasons for optimism. Gil still has good velocity, sitting 95.3 mph on his fourseamer in 2026, though that’s down over a full mile per hour from his peak a few years back. He has good riding action on the pitch at the top of the zone, along with plus extension. His slider and changeup are both quality plus pitches. At his best he’s electric. He just hasn’t been able to stay on the mound long enough to get in a groove the past two years. His command has never been particularly good, and his walk rates have spiked as the injuries took their toll, but he’ll throw enough strikes to make it work if healthy.

We’ll be curious to hear what Tigers’ president of baseball operations, Scott Harris, has to say about this acquisition. There’s a very good argument that Gil would be better off as a reliever. He topped out at 98.4 mph in 2026, despite the ongoing back troubles. If he can sit 97-98 mph in short bursts he’d be pretty electric with a plus slider-changeup combination. At the same time, he can come to camp as starting depth if needed as well.

Hopefully the medicals come back clean. The Tigers have not had much success keeping their pitchers healthy at any level of the organization. That’s a leaguewide problem, but the Tigers have had it worse than many if we put the whole farm system into the equation. The club has already made changes this offseason, hiring Scott Peters as their new medical director and Jeremiah Randall as head athletic trainer and physical therapist, so there’s clearly an emphasis on trying to address the problem.

Ultimately, this is a small, low risk move of the sort Harris favors. Yet Gil has a lot of talent if his body will just cooperate and the club could come out way ahead with this signing if they can get him right.

tigers.headline: Assessing the Tigers payroll in the wake of Troy Melton’s extension
tigers.body:
Detroit Tigers CEO and Chairman Chris Ilitch, manager A.J. Hinch and President of Baseball Operations Scott Harris and talk during Spring Training Tuesday, February 21, 2023. Tigers9 022123 Kd3999 | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

While the deal isn’t fully official until the medicals are completed, the Detroit Tigers have come to terms with right-handed starting pitcher Troy Melton on a long-term extension offer. The deal reportedly guarantees Melton six years and $46.5 million, with incentives and a club option for the 2033 season that could take the contract to a total of $80 million over seven years.

This is a pretty smart decision from both the Tigers and the 25-year-old Melton. Our thoughts quickly turned to potential extensions for talented youngsters like Jackson Jobe and Max Clark. The club already has AL Rookie of the Year Kevin McGonigle, as well as infielder Colt Keith signed to long-term extensions. It will be interesting to see if the Tigers pursue extensions with their other talented young players prior to the December 1 lockout of the players by MLB owners. They don’t want to get stuck with too much guaranteed money on the books for the long haul, but at the same time these contracts are certainly very team friendly as long as the players involved produce as expected.

Our next thought was how this sets up the Tigers payroll for 2027. The Tigers entered the 2026 season with a payroll that was pushing towards the $244 million luxury tax threshold. However, after trading away three of their most expensive players in Tarik Skubal, Casey Mize, and Jake Rogers, all of whom were in their final year of arbitration eligibility prior to free agency, the final estimated Tigers payroll for 2026 came down to $195 million according to FanGraphs.

FanGraphs’ Roster Resource now estimates the Tigers’ 2027 Opening Day payroll at $169 million in the wake of Melton’s extension. That total would’ve put the Tigers 15th most in payroll in the major leagues in 2026, right in the middle. These are the salaries for their free agent deals and extensions on the books for 2027.

Framber Valdez – $47.5M

Javier Báez – $24M

Emilio Pagán – $11.5M

Kyle Finnegan – $10M

Drew Anderson – $8M

Troy Melton – $7.75M

Colt Keith – $4.77M

Kevin McGonigle – $2.75M

Jacob Waguespack – $1.3M

In addition, the Tigers do have a few arbitration eligible players estimated to make over $5 million in 2027. Riley Greene is estimated to earn $9.3 million, while Spencer Torkelson is estimated at $7.7 million for the 2027 season. Those two players are under team control for 2027-2028, and will then be free agents in 2029.

Zach McKinstry is estimated to make $5 million next season, while both Will Vest and Kerry Carpenter are estimated to make $4.4 million and $4.1 million, respectively.

So, looking forward to the rest of the offseason, the Tigers are still in fine shape to go make a big signing or just continue to build up their pitching staff and possibly hunt for a better bat in a part-time role. Ihey were willing to spend something like $240 million in 2026. That doesn’t mean they’re planning on keeping payroll that high year after year, but it seems likely they could add another $30-40 million in payroll this offseason and still be well short of their 2026 Opening Day payroll projection.

There’s room to spend. It’s more a question of a lack of major impact players that fit this offseason. Presumably there’s also some trepidation about signing any big free agent deals with so much up in the air this offseason. With the CBA negotiations and lockout coming, most teams would prefer certainty as to what the sports rules and payrolls are going to look like under the next CBA before making any huge commitments. Some teams will obviously make exceptions for Tarik Skubal and a handful of other top free agents, but the Tigers don’t seem like they’re going to be involved with those players.

Still it’s interesting to consider the Tigers payroll situation in light of the possibility that the owners do get their way and there’s a cap and floor instituted for 2028 as proposed. Under the owners’ most recent proposal, the floor would be $180.2 million against a hard cap of $258.2 million. Part of that would involve smaller market teams like the Tigers getting more in revenue sharing money, but actually being required to spend up to that $180.2 million level. Since the Tigers were willing to spend roughly $240 million for the 2026 season, with additional league revenue coming in they would likely be in a position to spend close to that level on a yearly basis going forward.

The Tigers have their second biggest annual salary coming off the books after 2027 as Javier Báez reaches free agency. That takes $24 million off the payroll heading into 2028. And, should Framber Valdez bounce back in year two in Detroit with a good season, there’s a fair chance he would choose to decline his 2028 player option with the Tigers, worth $35 million, and head back to free agency. A cap and floor system might have some impact on Valdez’s desire to return to free agency a year early as well. Even so, while the Tigers’ expenses will increase elsewhere as players get raises and then reach arbitration, there is plenty of money bound to come off the books in the next few seasons as well.

Obviously, this is speculative as there’s nothing to suggest the players are going to give the owners what they want in the CBA negotiations. Still, thinking through the general possibilities shows the Tigers in pretty good shape going forward whether a cap and floor system is put in place or not. They could clearly afford even a $400 million offer to Tarik Skubal if they thought that was the best way to allocate their payroll. With several talented younger players already locked up on long-term deals, minimal major commitments to older players, and with a still good farm system brewing up more major league talent to come, the Tigers future looks pretty bright if the front office can finally make the right moves to put them seriously into contention on a yearly basis.

tigers.headline: Tigers sign RHP Troy Melton to a six-year extension
tigers.body:
CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 20: Troy Melton #52 of the Detroit Tigers delivers a pitch against the Chicago White Sox at Rate Field on September 20, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Jayden Mack/Getty Images) | Getty Images

While we were waiting for non-tender deadline news, and there was none involving the Tigers, who tendered contracts to all eligible players other than Matt Vierling, who was already DFA’d on Tuesday, the club had other business instead. Multiple reports emerged on Friday evening that the Tigers have inked right-hander Troy Melton to a six-year contract extension that guarantees him $46.5 million with incentives and a club option for 2033 that could max out at $80 million over seven years. The deal is still pending a physical and not officially announced yet.

The hard-throwing right-hander will turn 26 years old in about two weeks. He has one year and 68 days of MLB service time currently, so this deal arrives as Melton was still five full seasons from free agency. Exchanging an extra year until he’ll reach free agency, and potentially two years if the Tigers use their club option, to guarantee himself at least $46.5 million is a pretty good deal for both sides. Melton wouldn’t have reached free agency until he was headed into his age 31 season, and with pitcher injuries being what they are, there’s always the risk that he wouldn’t be as valuable by that point in his career.

From the Tigers’ perspective, they locked up six years of Melton at less than eight million a season, a bargain for a pitcher who is on track to be worth roughly 2 WAR per season if he continues on his current track. Of course, the Tigers, and no doubt Melton himself, expect continued improvements in the years ahead. There are plenty of incentives that could make the deal much more lucrative for Melton, but if he earns them the Tigers won’t have any problem paying him extra. With a 96-97 mph fastball with big extension that can reach triple digits, along with a deep and developing arsenal of pitches including a sinker, cutter, slider, curveball, and splitter, the potential here is pretty enormous. Melton just hasn’t found the strikeout touch consistently to take him into the upper tiers of starting pitchers around the league quite yet.

2026 was Melton’s first full season as a major leaguer after debuting in the second half of 2025 in a mixed role that included starts and high leverage relief appearances, and some good performances in the postseason. This season didn’t get off to a good start as Melton had some elbow inflammation in spring camp. The Tigers shut him down and took their time, getting him back on the mound in late May.

Melton went on to make 20 starts totaling 114.1 innings pitched. He posted a 2.76 ERA and a 4.09 FIP over that span. He keeps balanced splits, leaning on that deep repertoire of pitches. With more consistency from his good slider-split combination, he should be able to strike out more hitters. For now, the fact that he attacks the zone aggressively and doesn’t issue many walks, while controlling contact, is a great foundation to build on going forward.

His season didn’t end well, as his performance fell off in late August and into September. Eventually he was shut down after a start on September 20 with forearm tightness and general arm fatigue. Reports have since emerged that he’d avoided any serious injury. The Tigers must be pretty convinced in his medicals to have extended the extension offer, and perhaps those issues during the season convinced Melton that it was a good idea to come to an agreement and guarantee himself the money now.

One also wonders what this says about the status of Jackson Jobe and Max Clark, two other highly talented youngsters who have shown some nice flashes in the major leagues but are really just getting started. It will be interesting to see if this is just the first in a flurry of extensions designed to provide stability and cost certainty with the Tigers top young players just as the sport heads into an extremely uncertain time with the lockout and CBA negotiations looming.
